paragraphs.source_en: Being a cat, my knowledge of the world is limited, and it is only recently that I first had the honor of beholding such a thing as a go board. The more I think about it, the stranger the contrivance seems. They take a square board and cramp it into many narrow little squares, then crowd it with black and white stones until the sight of it dazzles the eyes. After that they make a great commotion about winning and losing, living and dying, dripping oily sweat all the while. At most, it is an area of about one square foot. One swipe of my cat’s paw would instantly scatter the whole thing into confusion. It is just like the old saying: “Bound upright, it is a thatched hut; scattered apart, it is a desolate field.” It is truly an idle game that wastes one’s labor. It would be far easier simply to fold one’s arms and gaze at the board. Nor is that all. During the first thirty or forty moves the arrangement of the stones is not especially offensive to the eye, but once the fate of the realm is about to be decided and I look again, good heavens! It is a sight to stir one’s pity: white stones and black stones are packed so tightly together that they seem about to spill off the board, and they cry out in distress; cramped as they are, they cannot ask the other side to yield room, and though they obstruct one another they have no right to order the gentleman in front to withdraw, so they can do nothing but resign themselves to fate and cling motionless to their places. Since go was invented by human beings, if human tastes are expressed upon the board, then the fate of these immobile stones may fairly be said to reflect the narrow-minded nature of mankind. If human nature can be inferred from the fate of go stones, then one must say that mankind, just as it refuses at all costs to step beyond the two legs on which it stands, also likes to mark off its own territory with a little knife and shrink its vast world. In a word, one might describe mankind as an animal that goes out of its way to seek suffering.

paragraphs.source_en: The ever-easygoing Meitei and the Zen-minded Dokusen, for reasons known only to themselves, had on this day of all days dragged the old go board from the cupboard and begun this still more heat-oppressive foolery. Since the two were, after all, an extraordinary pair, from the outset each adopted erratic moves of his own, and the white and black stones were set down in free disorder across the board; but the board’s space is finite, and each stone fills one crossing of its horizontal and vertical lines, so however easygoing or Zen-inspired they might be, it was only natural that in the end things should become more and more cramped.
